notes: Ruling slot 23 holds the Sangkum (Sihanouk's royalist movement; throne vacant, Queen Kossamak symbolic), so the House of Norodom has no separate slot. Lon Nol/Sirik Matak cabinet in 13, Khmer Serei in 0, army in 22. Pro-Hanoi Pracheachon in 4, Maoist CPK (Khmer Rouge) in 19. Islamic slots use Cham institutions; slot 9 is a small Shia trader circle.

0.name: Khmer Serei
0.text:
The Khmer Serei, the 'Free Khmer', is the armed exile movement of Son Ngoc Thanh, the nationalist prime minister of 1945 who broke with the throne and has waged a low-level insurgency against Prince Sihanouk since the late 1950s. On 1 January 1970 it operates from camps along the Thai border and among the Khmer Krom of South Vietnam, where its fighters are trained and paid by American Special Forces.

The movement wants Sihanouk removed, the monarchy replaced by a republic and Cambodia brought openly into the anti-communist camp beside Saigon, Bangkok and Washington. Its leverage lies in its armed Khmer Krom units, its radio propaganda and quiet sympathy among officers who resent the Prince's tolerance of Vietnamese communist sanctuaries.

1.name: Kanakpak Sereipheap
1.text:
The Liberal Party was founded in 1946 by Prince Norodom Norindeth as the voice of conservative notables, landowners and officials who favoured gradual independence in partnership with France. Repeatedly defeated by the Democrats, it was absorbed into Prince Sihanouk's Sangkum in 1955 and has no formal existence on 1 January 1970, but its families still fill the upper ranks of the court and the provincial administration.

Its heirs stand for order, property, Buddhism and the dignity of the royal family, distrust the Prince's flirtation with Peking and Hanoi, and favour quiet cooperation with France and the West. Their influence lies in patronage networks, the senior civil service and the Council of the Kingdom rather than in any mass following.

2.name: Krom Pracheathipatey
2.text:
The Democratic Party was founded in 1946 by Prince Sisowath Youtevong and won every election of the late 1940s on a platform of constitutional government and full independence. Harassed by the palace, it was broken in the 1955 elections and dissolved itself into the Sangkum in 1957. On 1 January 1970 it survives as a memory and a network of veterans scattered through the schools, the bar and the civil service.

The Democrats stand for parliamentary sovereignty, a monarchy that reigns but does not rule, civil liberties and honest administration. They are wary of both blocs, critical of the Prince's personal rule and of corruption at court, and draw on the urban educated class, students and junior officials who chafe under Sangkum conformity.

3.name: Le Cercle de Phnom Penh
3.text:
Le Cercle de Phnom Penh is the loose circle of French-educated teachers, lecturers and journalists in the capital who carry the left wing of the old Democratic Party into the Sangkum era. Its best-known figure is Keng Vannsak, the linguist who led the Democrats' left in 1955 and has since taught a generation of students in Phnom Penh.

The circle argues for a parliamentary, socially reforming Cambodia: land for the peasants, free trade unions, honest elections and an end to palace patronage. It rejects both Sihanouk's personal rule and the armed path of the maquis, looks to French socialism for its models and has influence mainly through lecture halls, lycée staff rooms and the capital's newspapers.

4.name: Krom Pracheachon
4.text:
The Pracheachon Group was created in 1954 as the legal front of the Khmer communists trained by the Viet Minh, contesting the 1955 and 1958 elections before police repression shattered it; its leader Non Suon has been in prison since 1962. On 1 January 1970 its surviving cadres are in jail, in hiding, or among the Khmer communists regrouped in North Vietnam since 1954, awaiting their return under Hanoi's protection.

The group follows the Vietnamese Workers' Party line: a united front with Sihanouk's neutralism, support for the Vietnamese war against the Americans and a gradual road to socialism. It looks to Hanoi and Moscow, distrusts the Maoist leadership of the Cambodian party, and its leverage rests on Vietnamese protection and veteran prestige.

5.name: Union Générale des Étudiants Khmers
5.text:
The General Union of Khmer Students gathers the Cambodian students of Paris and other French universities, heir to the student associations of the 1950s in which Saloth Sar, Ieng Sary and Khieu Samphan first studied Marxism. On 1 January 1970 it is a hotbed of anti-imperialist agitation, closely watched by the Cambodian embassy and courted by the French left.

Its members denounce the Sangkum as feudal and corrupt, condemn the American war in Vietnam and admire the Chinese Cultural Revolution and the guerrillas of the Cambodian maquis. Its influence lies in recruitment: returning graduates fill lycée classrooms in Phnom Penh, and the most radical slip into the forests to join the clandestine party.

6.name: Le Clan Monique
6.text:
Le Clan Monique is the name Phnom Penh gives to the family and clients of Princess Monique, Sihanouk's consort, led by her half-brother Oum Mannorine, who holds a key post over the security services. The clan grows rich on monopolies, the new state casino and the trade carrying rice and arms from the port of Sihanoukville to the Vietnamese communist sanctuaries along the border.

Its interest is the status quo: the Prince's personal rule, the patronage economy and close ties with Hanoi and Peking that keep the profitable supply routes open. It loathes Lon Nol, Sirik Matak and the Americans, and its leverage lies entirely in its access to the Prince, his consort and the palace.

7.name: Jeunesse Socialiste Royale Khmère
7.text:
The Royal Khmer Socialist Youth is the Sangkum's uniformed youth organization, founded in 1957 to drill schoolchildren, students and young civil servants in loyalty to Prince Sihanouk and his Buddhist socialism. On 1 January 1970 it exists in every province, marches at national festivals and supplies auxiliaries for public works and village vigilance.

It embodies the anti-American, pro-Chinese face of the regime: it rallies against 'imperialist aggression' from Saigon and Bangkok, mobilizes for the Prince's foreign policy and polices dissent in schools. Its leverage lies in numbers and in the patronage of officials around the palace, though many members are bored conscripts rather than true believers.

8.name: Kan Imam San
8.text:
The Imam San community is a traditionalist branch of Cambodia's Cham Muslims centred on Oudong and Kampong Chhnang, devoted to the memory of Imam San, a nineteenth-century Cham religious leader honoured by the Khmer court. On 1 January 1970 it keeps its own religious leaders and calendar of rites and remains close to the royal palace, which receives its delegations at festivals.

The community prays mainly on Fridays, preserves Cham script and older customs, and resists the Malay-trained reformers who call its practices un-Islamic. It is loyal to Sihanouk, wary of politics beyond the village, and its weight lies in religious legitimacy among rural Cham and its old ties to the crown.

9.name: Les Marchands Khojas
9.text:
Les Marchands Khojas are a handful of Shia trading families from Gujarat and Bombay who keep textile and jewellery shops around Phnom Penh's markets, part of the small South Asian commercial community that arrived under the French protectorate. They maintain a private prayer hall, follow Twelver clerics in Bombay and Najaf, and stand apart from the Sunni Cham majority.

Outwardly they are cautious and loyal to whatever government protects commerce, but some younger men follow the sermons of exiled Najaf clerics calling for government by learned jurists. Their leverage is money: credit networks reaching Saigon, Bangkok and Bombay, and links to Shia communities across the Indian Ocean.

10.name: Mupti Kampuchea
10.english: Office of the Mufti of Cambodia
10.text:
The Office of the Mufti heads the official hierarchy of Cambodia's Cham and Malay Muslims, a system of royal appointment in which the mufti and his deputies, the tuon pake and the raja kalik, are confirmed by the crown and preside over mosques, customary courts and religious schools. On 1 January 1970 it speaks for some two hundred thousand believers along the Mekong and Tonle Sap.

The hierarchy preaches loyalty to the throne and to Prince Sihanouk, who praises the Cham as a loyal minority, and keeps practice within Shafi'i tradition and royal protocol. It cultivates links with Malaysia and Mecca for scholarships and pilgrimage, and its influence lies in appointments, mosque endowments and Cham village votes delivered to the Sangkum.

11.name: Front de Libération du Champa
11.english: Front for the Liberation of Champa
11.text:
The Front for the Liberation of Champa is the Cham wing of FULRO, the alliance of highland and Cham peoples fighting for autonomy from Saigon. Its leader Les Kosem is a Cham officer of the Cambodian army who runs training camps on Cambodian soil with the knowledge of senior commanders, among them Lon Nol.

The front dreams of restoring Champa, the old kingdom swallowed by the Vietnamese, and mixes ethnic nationalism with a call to defend Islam against Vietnamese domination of every stripe. It is anti-communist and anti-Vietnamese, armed and secretive, and its leverage lies in its fighters, its friends in the Cambodian officer corps and the grievances of Cham communities on both sides of the border.

12.name: Kaum Muda
12.text:
Kaum Muda, the 'young group', is the reformist movement among Cambodian Cham Muslims led by teachers trained in Kelantan, Mecca and Cairo, who challenge the customary religion of village elders and the royal hierarchy. By 1970 its preachers run Qur'an schools in Phnom Penh and the riverside villages of Kampong Cham and send students abroad on Malaysian and Arab scholarships.

The reformers call for a purified Sunni practice based on scripture, Arabic learning and Muslim solidarity across Southeast Asia, while seeking a respectable place for Islam inside the Cambodian state. They avoid confrontation with the Prince and draw their strength from youth, literacy and patrons in Malaysia and the Arab world.

13.name: Gouvernement de Sauvetage
13.text:
The Government of Salvation is the cabinet formed in August 1969 under General Lon Nol, with Prince Sisowath Sirik Matak as first deputy prime minister, after the National Assembly pressed Prince Sihanouk to accept a government drawn from the right of the Sangkum. On 1 January 1970 Lon Nol is in France for medical treatment and Sirik Matak runs the cabinet in his place.

The cabinet presents itself as neutral and non-partisan, but its austerity, denationalization of banks and trade and crackdown on the Vietnamese communist supply trade set it against the Prince's circle. Its leverage lies in the ministries, the army and the National Assembly majority that installed it.

14.name: Mohanikay
14.text:
The Maha Nikaya is the larger of Cambodia's two Buddhist orders, counting the great majority of the kingdom's monks and village pagodas. Its supreme patriarch Chuon Nath, who died in 1969, shaped modern Khmer through his dictionary and made the order a pillar of national identity; on 1 January 1970 its hierarchy remains close to the throne and the Sangkum.

The order teaches respect for authority, merit-making and harmony between the sangha and the state, and lends its blessing to Sihanouk's Buddhist socialism. It is wary of both communism and Western materialism. Its leverage is immense but indirect: every village pagoda is a school, a meeting hall and a voice that peasants trust more than any official.

15.name: Les Maîtres du Riz
15.text:
Les Maîtres du Riz are the Sino-Khmer merchant houses, rice millers and moneylenders who dominate Cambodia's trade, organized through Teochew, Cantonese, Hokkien, Hakka and Hainanese associations in Phnom Penh, Battambang and Kampot. Since the nationalization of banking and foreign trade in 1963 they work through state agencies, smuggling and partnerships with officials.

They want the state monopolies dismantled, private banks restored and order kept in the countryside, and they finance whoever can deliver it. Some profit from rice sales to the Vietnamese communists; others hope Sirik Matak's reforms will reopen legitimate trade. Their leverage is credit: almost every peasant harvest in the kingdom passes through their scales.

16.name: Libre Entreprise
16.text:
Libre Entreprise is the circle of bankers, importers, young economists and French-trained officials pushing to undo the nationalization of banks, insurance and foreign trade decreed in 1963. Its patron is Prince Sisowath Sirik Matak, who has made denationalization the centrepiece of his work in the Government of Salvation since August 1969.

The group blames state monopolies and the rejection of American aid for empty shelves, smuggling and stagnation, and calls for private banking, foreign investment and a return of Western aid. It is small but well placed in the economic ministries, the business community and the Phnom Penh press, where it argues that only an open economy can save the kingdom's finances.

17.name: Conservation d'Angkor
17.text:
Angkor Conservation is the Siem Reap service charged since 1908 with protecting the temples of Angkor, run since 1960 by the French archaeologist Bernard-Philippe Groslier for the École française d'Extrême-Orient. On 1 January 1970 its engineers and hundreds of Khmer workers rebuild monuments stone by stone and manage the forests, moats and reservoirs around the ancient capital.

Its people argue that the temples, the Tonle Sap and the northern forests are a national patrimony to be protected from looting, logging and reckless development, and they quietly fear the war spilling over the border. Their leverage is prestige: Angkor is the emblem on the flag and the heart of Sihanouk's national pride.

18.name: Socialisme Khmer
18.text:
Socialisme Khmer is the technocratic wing of the Sangkum that built the state economy of the 1960s: the nationalized banks, the state trading company and the factories raised with Chinese, Czechoslovak and French aid. Its foremost figure is Son Sann, longtime governor of the National Bank and prime minister in 1967–68.

Its adherents defend Sihanouk's Buddhist socialism as a Khmer middle way between capitalism and communism: state ownership of key sectors, cooperatives for peasants, welfare inspired by the dharma and strict neutrality between the blocs. They resent the right's denationalization drive, and their leverage lies in the state enterprises, the planning offices and the Prince's ear.

19.name: Pak Kommunist Kampuchea
19.text:
The Communist Party of Kampuchea is the clandestine party Sihanouk calls the 'Khmers Rouges', renamed in 1966 and led by its secretary Saloth Sar with Nuon Chea and Ieng Sary. After the Samlaut uprising of 1967 it launched armed struggle in January 1968; on 1 January 1970 its few thousand guerrillas hold forest bases in the north-east and the Cardamoms, joined by the former deputies Khieu Samphan, Hou Yuon and Hu Nim.

Inspired by Mao's China and suspicious of Vietnamese tutelage, it preaches peasant revolution, self-reliance and the destruction of the feudal Sangkum order. It keeps its own name secret and draws strength from the poorest upland villages, highland minorities and radicalized teachers.

20.name: Les Députés de 1966
20.text:
Les Députés de 1966 are the National Assembly members elected in September 1966, the first Sangkum election in which Prince Sihanouk did not hand-pick the candidates. Dominated by provincial notables, merchants and officers, the Assembly chose Lon Nol as prime minister in 1966 and pressed for the Government of Salvation in 1969; its president is Cheng Heng.

The deputies voice the anger of the towns and provinces at corruption around the palace, the economic slump and the Vietnamese communist troops encamped on Khmer soil. Their language is anti-Vietnamese and increasingly anti-Sihanouk, and their leverage lies in the Assembly's power over ministers and in the crowds of students and officials they can rally.

21.name: Khmer Kampuchea Krom
21.text:
The Khmer Kampuchea Krom is a militant movement of ethnic Khmers from the Mekong Delta of South Vietnam, formed in the 1960s to defend Khmer Krom villages and pagodas against Vietnamese assimilation. Its armed bands, trained and paid by American Special Forces, serve in camps along the border, and Lon Nol, who dreams of a greater Khmer nation, protects it from inside the Cambodian army.

The movement preaches an ethnic nationalism of blood and soil, the recovery of Kampuchea Krom, hatred of Vietnamese of every political colour and anti-communism in the service of the race. It is small, fanatical and armed, and its leverage lies in seasoned fighters, delta monks and a patron at the top of the officer corps.

22.name: Forces Armées Royales Khmères
22.text:
The Royal Khmer Armed Forces number about 35,000 men, equipped with a mix of French, Chinese and Soviet weapons since Sihanouk renounced American aid in 1963. General Lon Nol, prime minister and long-serving defence minister, is their master, and officers loyal to him hold the key commands around Phnom Penh.

The officer corps is frustrated by low pay, obsolete equipment and the presence of tens of thousands of Vietnamese communist troops in border sanctuaries the army is forbidden to touch. It is anti-communist and increasingly pro-American, and its leverage is decisive: it alone controls force in a kingdom where the Prince's authority rests on prestige.

23.name: Sangkum Reastr Niyum
23.text:
The People's Socialist Community, the Sangkum, is the national movement founded in 1955 by Norodom Sihanouk after he abdicated the throne to enter politics. It absorbed every legal party and has held every seat in the National Assembly since; Sihanouk has ruled as head of state since 1960, while his mother Queen Kossamak embodies the vacant crown.

The Sangkum preaches Buddhist socialism, loyalty to the royal family and strict neutrality, balancing Peking, Hanoi and Paris against Washington and Bangkok. Its strength is the Prince himself: his radio speeches, provincial tours and immense prestige among the peasantry hold together a movement that is in fact a coalition of rival clans, generals and technocrats.
